title: Fewer Subs, Bigger Scope Risk: How Trade Shortages Hit GC Bids in 2026
summary: With 439,000 open trade positions, subs are picking their bids carefully and billing every gap. Here's how GCs reduce scope risk in 2026.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- There are 439,000 unfilled trade positions in North America in 2026. Electrician job postings are up 50.8% and plumber postings up 54.1% in H1 2026 alone.
- When subs have leverage, they pick the cleanest bids. Vague scope sheets finish last.
- "Errors and omissions in contract documents" ranks as the leading cause of construction disputes in North America, per Arcadis.
- Scope gaps that used to get absorbed on a gentleman's agreement now get billed. Every time.
- GCs who close scope gaps before bid day win more work and defend their margins better.


Subs are busier than they have been in a decade. That changes how they respond to your invitations to bid. It changes what they price. And it changes what they will and will not absorb when a scope gap surfaces in the field.


If your scope sheets are still built the same way they were five years ago, your exposure is bigger than you think.


## The Labor Market Is Reshaping Pre-Construction Risk


The numbers are concrete. There are 439,000 unfilled trade positions across North America in 2026. Electrician job postings rose 50.8% in H1 2026. Plumber postings rose 54.1% in the same period, according to ConTech Roundup data.


What does that mean for a GC trying to build a competitive bid? It means fewer qualified subs responding. It means the ones who do respond are choosing which jobs to price. And it means the best subs are walking away from bids that look unclear, risky, or underspecified.


As one Estimating Manager at a Canadian ICI general contractor put it: *"We have fewer subs who operate on a gentleman's agreement. They've become more quick to clarify that they're not including that one piece of scope."*


That is not a complaint about subs. That is a market signal. Subs with full backlogs do not need to absorb ambiguous scope. They price what is explicit and exclude everything else.


## What "Errors and Omissions" Actually Cost GCs


The 2024 Arcadis Global Construction Disputes Report puts the average North American construction dispute value at $60.1 million. "Errors and omissions in contract documents" ranks as the leading cause of those disputes in North America. This is not a one-year anomaly. Arcadis has tracked this pattern across multiple reporting cycles.


The mechanism is straightforward. Scope gaps produce change orders. Change orders produce disputes. Disputes erode margin and damage owner relationships.


A 2018 study by PlanGrid and FMI estimated that rework tied to miscommunication and bad project data cost the U.S. construction industry $31.3 billion. Communication breakdowns alone accounted for 26% of that rework. Bad project data accounted for another 22%.


Those numbers are several years old. The problem has not gotten smaller.


## Scope Gaps Don't Happen by Accident


The core argument in Provision's[Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/trade-specific-scope-gaps) is worth repeating here: scope gaps are caused, not random. They follow a small set of predictable patterns. When you know the patterns, you can close them before bid day.


Three of the most common causes are:


1. **Boilerplate scope sheets used without review.** "As per plans and specs" is the most-cited anti-pattern in GC scope writing. It tells a sub nothing specific. It gives them every reason to exclude ambiguous items.
2. **Copy-paste from a previous similar job.** The last hospital may have had the same division breakdown as this one. But the spec sections are different, the drawings are different, and the sub pricing it today is not the same sub who worked through the ambiguity on that last job.
3. **Junior estimators stuffing previous scopes verbatim.** A scope sheet built by someone who has never walked the documents is a scope sheet built for someone else's project.


These habits compound in a tight labor market. When you only get two or three responses to an ITB, you have no room to negotiate out a scope gap at buyout. You take what you get.


## Trade-Specific Scope Risk Is Getting Worse


Some of the highest-risk scope gaps are trade-specific. They appear in the same spots on nearly every project. The ones that cause the most pain tend to be the ones that look small until they aren't.


### MEP: Where the Dollars Accumulate Fast


MEP trades are among the hardest to source right now. That makes MEP scope gaps especially dangerous. Common gaps include:


- Generator field conditioning costs, which often appear nowhere in the drawings and fall into a gray zone between electrical and mechanical
- Motor starters, excluded by default unless the scope explicitly requires them
- Fire-rated louvres, which live at the intersection of mechanical and envelope and get claimed by neither
- Lighting controls, which specs may call out but scope sheets often miss
- The trench: who provides it, who coordinates with who, and what the tolerance expectations are


One Pre-Construction Lead at a Top-ENR Canadian GC described the exposure bluntly: *"If you miss anything, they'll bill it."*


### Envelope and Roofing


Roof cover board is a $400,000 gap waiting to happen. It happened on a $50M project, and the GC recovered it only through a relational concession from the sub. That is not a risk management strategy. That is luck.


Masonry-to-storefront flashings, caulking responsibilities between interior and exterior, and fire-stopping at penetrations are all items that fall through the cracks when scope sheets rely on "as per plans and specs" language.


### Specialty and Hospital Work


Lead-lined glass in a hospital imaging suite cost one GC $300,000 when it was omitted from the mechanical scope and absorbed under "readily inferable" language. That phrase, "readily inferable," is doing a lot of work in GC subcontracts right now. As a Senior PM at a Canadian ICI GC noted: *"Our construction management clients expect us to find the scope gaps in the design too now. They expect us to be designers and engineers."*


If subs are increasingly unwilling to absorb ambiguous items, GCs are absorbing them instead.


## The Buyout Window Is Narrowing


In a normal market, GCs have some negotiating room at buyout. They can work through scope gaps with subs, clarify inclusions and exclusions, and bridge the difference on items that neither party priced clearly.


That window is tighter in 2026. Subs who have full backlogs do not negotiate as much. They hold their price or they walk. That means scope gaps that used to get resolved at buyout are now either absorbed by the GC or become change orders mid-project.


Change orders on commercial work typically run 8–14% of project cost, according to Navigant research republished by AIA. On projects with weak scope, that number exceeds 25%.


The math is not complicated. A $20M project with a 10% change order rate is a $2M exposure. If two or three of those change orders trace back to scope gaps that were visible in the drawings before bid day, that is avoidable margin loss.


## What Separates GCs Who Win from GCs Who Lose Coverage


The[Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/trade-specific-scope-gaps) identifies eight habits that separate firms with strong margins from firms that absorb gaps. Several of them are directly relevant to what a tighter labor market demands.


### Habit 1: Drawings-First, Not Boilerplate-First


Start from the drawings and specs for this project. Use your template as a starting point, not an ending point. Every scope sheet should reference specific drawing sheets and spec sections, not generic incorporation language.


### Habit 3: Front-Load the Buyout Conversations


If you know a trade is tight, start the buyout conversation before bid day. Find out what the sub is and is not planning to include. That conversation shapes how you write the scope and what you need to close before you go to contract.


### Habit 7: Clarifications, Not Just Exclusions


An exclusion list tells you what a sub is not doing. A clarification list tells you what they are doing and how. In a tight market, clarifications are more useful. They give you a foundation for a scope conversation that actually resolves ambiguity.


### Habit 8: The Pre-Issue Scope Review Checkpoint


Build a checkpoint before you issue scope sheets. Someone other than the estimator who built the sheet should read it against the drawings. Not for formatting. For coverage. For the items that look like they should be in there but are not.


As one Pre-Construction Lead at a Top-ENR Canadian GC explained: *"It's descriptive: bread, put it on a plate, use the open jar. You have to get to that level of detail or else they'll just be like, 'you didn't tell us that.'"*

## What to Do Before Your Next Bid


You cannot fix the labor shortage. But you can close the scope gaps that the shortage makes expensive. Here is a practical checklist for your next bid cycle:


1. **Audit your ITB list for thin coverage.** Which trades have only one or two qualified subs responding? Those are your highest-risk items.
2. **Pull every scope sheet that uses "as per plans and specs" as a primary reference.** Replace it with specific drawing sheets and spec sections.
3. **Run a pre-issue review on MEP, envelope, and specialty scopes.** These are the highest-frequency gap locations.
4. **Start buyout conversations before bid day on tight trades.** Find out what subs are planning to include before you price to your owner.
5. **Document clarifications, not just exclusions.** An explicit inclusion list is more useful than a generic laundry list of carve-outs.


The GCs who protect margin in 2026 are not the ones with the most subs on their list. They are the ones with the most complete scope sheets. That is the competitive advantage that a tight labor market rewards.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### How does the trade labor shortage increase scope risk for GCs?


When fewer subs respond to an ITB, GCs have less leverage at buyout. Subs with full backlogs are more likely to price only what is explicitly in the scope sheet and exclude everything else. Scope gaps that previously got absorbed on informal agreements now become change orders or disputes.


### What trades carry the most scope gap risk in 2026?


MEP trades are under the most strain, with electrician and plumber job postings up over 50% in H1 2026. Specialty trades like curtainwall, elevator, and hospital equipment work also carry high scope risk. Envelope work, including roofing and storefront, is a consistent source of large missed items.


### What does "readily inferable" language mean for GC risk?


Readily inferable language in subcontracts requires subs to include work that a reasonable contractor would consider necessary, even if not explicitly called out. As subs become more selective and sophisticated, they are quicker to push back on this language. That pushes the exposure back to the GC.


### What is the most common scope writing mistake GCs make?


"As per plans and specs" is the most cited scope writing anti-pattern. It gives subs no specific guidance on what to include and creates maximum ambiguity at buyout. Specific drawing sheet references and spec section callouts reduce that ambiguity and reduce change order exposure.


### How accurate is AI for generating construction scope of work packages?


Provision's Scope Agent achieves 97% match accuracy on scope item extraction in internal validation testing. Human estimators on the same exercise averaged 91.3% at roughly four days per project. The key difference is that purpose-built construction AI reads drawings, specs, and contracts together, the way a scope package actually needs to be built.


### How much do change orders typically cost on commercial projects?


Research from Navigant, republished by AIA, puts change orders at 8–14% of project cost on typical commercial work. On projects with weak or incomplete scope, that figure can exceed 25%. On a $20M project, that is $2M or more in potential exposure.
